title: Microplastics

endcard.line: Pictures: Gabriele85 (CC0); Martin Wagner et al. (CC BY 4.0)

segments.say: Any piece of plastic smaller than five millimetres, about the size of a pencil eraser, has a name: a microplastic.
Some are made small on purpose, like the microbeads once added to face washes and toothpastes. Most break off bigger things, like bottles, bags and fishing nets.
Everyday life adds more: tyres wearing down on roads, fibres shed when synthetic clothes are washed, and litter slowly breaking apart.
Scientists now find them in river and sea sediments. America's ocean agency says they can harm ocean and aquatic life, though much about them is still unknown.
And they keep breaking down, into nanoplastics too small to see, which researchers think may risk both nature and human health.
India's answer starts at the source. Since the first of July twenty twenty-two, identified single-use plastic items with low use and high litter, like plastic cutlery and straws, are banned.
For GS Three, link microplastics to the plastic waste rules: the surest way to stop small plastic is to stop the big plastic it comes from.

sources: NOAA Ocean Service, 'What are microplastics?': plastic pieces less than five millimetres long, about the size of a pencil eraser; sources include larger pieces breaking apart, resin pellets and microbeads in health and beauty products such as cleansers and toothpastes; can be harmful to the ocean and aquatic life; not much is known yet about their impacts

Wikipedia, 'Microplastics' (read): primary microplastics are manufactured small; secondary microplastics come from the breakdown of larger items such as bottles, fishing nets, bags and tyre wear; fibres from washing synthetic clothing; nanoplastics are thought to be a risk to environmental and human health

PIB, 28 June 2022 (PRID 1837518): Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2021 (notified 12 August 2021) ban manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale and use of identified single-use plastic items with low utility and high littering potential from 1 July 2022; the list includes earbuds with plastic sticks, plastic cutlery, straws, thermocol for decoration and wrapping film around sweet boxes

quiz.q: What is the upper size limit for a microplastic?
quiz.why: NOAA: pieces less than five millimetres long.

quiz.q: A microplastic that breaks off a plastic bottle is called…
quiz.why: Secondary microplastics come from larger items breaking down.

quiz.q: From when did India ban identified single-use plastic items?
quiz.why: PIB: the ban took effect on 1 July 2022.

reviewNote: Facts are from NOAA, PIB and the Wikipedia article (for primary/secondary and nanoplastics). 'Once added to face washes' reflects that several countries have banned microbeads; the script avoids saying where. 'Food packaging' on the sources card comes from the Wikipedia list. Moving facts: research on health effects is moving fast; the script stays cautious.
